newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Sierra Leone truce agreed, further talks July 25.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone truce agreed, further talks July 25.

text.p: West African foreign ministers and envoys of Sierra Leone's military rulers agreed on Friday that there should be an immediate halt to all fighting throughout the battered nation.

A statement, read by Nigerian Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi after a second day of talks in Ivory Coast, said that the two sides agreed "to resolve all issues related to the Sierra Leone crisis peacefully". The two sides resolved to meet next Friday.

The statement said the junta team would return to Freetown to draft plans for restoring Sierra Leone to "constitutional order". It sidestepped the issue of whether Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, a civilian ousted on May 25, would return as president.
Asked if "constitutional order" implied Kabbah's reinstatement, junta spokesman Allieu Kamara told Reuters: "No, far from that."
Economic Community of West African States ministers at the talks -- Nigeria, Ivory Coast, Guinea and Ghana attended -- said this was the main aim of their diplomatic effort.

Nigerian troops, in Sierra Leone under a pre-coup defence pact, have clashed with junta forces and their rebel allies. So too have members of a Kamajor traditional hunter militia given extra powers by Kabbah -- a big grievance of the coup leaders.
Kamara said the truce deal meant the borders and the airport, currently closed by Nigerian troops, would reopen. "No more blockades. The airport will be open. No more hostilities."
Sierra Leone's neighbours decided in Guinea on June 26 to pursue dialogue and economic sanctions to persuade the junta to restore Kabbah, but they retained a military option.
Friday's statement said the two sides would "work towards early restoration of constitutional order and that a ceasefire should be established "immediately throughout Sierra Leone".

Members of the junta delegation called before the talks for Nigeria to let rebel leader Foday Sankoh, under effective house arrest in Nigeria, return to Sierra Leone. This wish was noted in the final statement.
Sankoh's name was included on the original Sierra Leone delegation list for this week's talks.
Asked if he would be present on July 25, delegation leader Pallo Bangura said: "Everything will be done to facilitate his participation in the process."

Corporal Tamba Gborie, who led the coup and installed Major Johnny Paul Koroma as military leader, said it would be impossible to strike a deal without Sankoh, who has been named Koroma's number two in the junta.
"You can't make any peace in Sierra Leone without Foday Sankoh," Gborie said.
According to the final statement, the Sierra Leone delegation "expressed deep regret at the loss of lives" in the coup and subsequent fighting.
A group of British charities said in a statement issued in London on Friday that over 30,000 people had fled to neighbouring states since May 25.
Witnesses in Freetown said hundreds of people had fled the capital since the latest flare-up in fighting at the weekend and in fear of failure at the talks.
